candidates.text:
Assorted things I've been mulling over regarding agents in the economy:

• Companies are in some sense the original superintelligence. It's often the case that they can use their amortized cognitive surplus to advance their interests against those of certain consumers: relative to the optimization capacity of companies, consumers can be inattentive, underinformed, irrational, etc. (Think, say, of some of the classic insurance upsells at the end of a booking process, which is typically priced substantially above what a regular policy would cost.) Herbert Simon introduced the idea of bounded rationality, and firms often end up benefiting from it. Thanks to personal agents, we will probably get somewhat more rational in how we engage with companies.

• How exactly will outcomes change? Well, certain kinds of price discrimination will work less well (how do coupons work if every agent hunts fastidiously for them?), and certain kinds of customer cross-subsidy will change (today, people who forget to cancel subscriptions subsidize those who don't). Taken across the economy as a whole, I'm not sure what the incidence of all of this will be.

• In corporate strategy, people have long debated the relative importance of distribution and product quality. Perhaps you've made something better, but does anyone know about it? Won't people just continue to buy the ACME Corp Mousetraps? Personal agents will, I think, act as a kind of structural subsidy for product quality. How would markets look different if individuals always spent at least 10 hours researching their purchases? On the margin, focusing on making a product better is, I think, going to become a more effective strategy for companies. This is good!

• It true, a corollary is that information about product quality will become more important and impactful. Today, most people have very limited ability to aggregate and integrate such data, but agents will have insatiable thirst for such signals. (It's often said that data is becoming more valuable because it helps in the training of models. That's obviously true, but I think there's a secondary way in which it's more valuable simply as a complement to cheaper intelligence.)

• A big question is whether agents will increase superstar effects (rational agents all settle on the same product) or increase dispersion (because everyone has slightly different tastes and preferences, which agents are good at eliciting, finally overcoming the artificial clustering we've been subjected to).

• Many internet companies have monetized demand routing, which is in turn often predicated on short attention spans. "I'll click on the first thing I see." This has led to some amount of inefficiency, as companies try to propitiate capricious ranking algorithms and incur various placement fees. It's not all deadweight loss (willingness to pay is itself a kind of signal, which is valuable to buyers), but it's not great. How will the nature and value of this routing change in a world of personal agents? I don't know the answer, but I think that the effects might be pretty big.

• Much of what I'm writing hinges on the assumption that personal agents will be on the consumer's side. I suspect that that will be the winning strategy, but whether it's true, and what it means to be true, involves a lot of other questions.

Taken as a whole, the market is a massively parallelized, decentralized, and highly imperfect value attribution machine, and, taking stock of all of the effects, it seems to me that the quality point may well be the biggest: that agents will change the nature of the backpropagation such that the rewards for better products increase. Maybe this is too optimistic, but I suspect (and hope) that companies that make things that they're proud of will feel that the universe is a little more partisan in their favor.

English: N + eight = Night
German: N + acht = Nacht
French: N + huit = Nuit
Spanish: N + ocho = Noche
Italian: N + otto = Notte

candidates.text:
This is a good article explaining how it all works. Gokul’s tweet fired up a storm recently on this. (Full disclosure I have once connected one company looking to sell data to a data broker; apart from the bit of commission, understanding how the ecosystem works itself was interesting) 

I do want to comment on a bit of irony that a lot of people say that there has been this massive schadenfraude with open source. Not just code but open source anything (writing, art, design whatever - that was FOSS or CC0 or so on). 
That those who put their work out did it for other humans and then these big labs came and monetised it all like vultures or something. 

Well; imagine if all your life you did work for a proprietary place (and got paid of course); the same thing is still happening with your work nevertheless. Your slack messages where you approved someone’s work is an eval now. Your workflows are training data, your design documents are are in Claude and GPTs training corpus now. And while you were paid originally for the work itself, you are not going to be paid freshly when all your past work gets reused as training material when your CEO goes and sells this to a lab. 

And I am not saying this in either positive or negative light; I’m quite ambivalent to this (yes I have the privilege to not have my immediate livelihood being destroyed by AI right now; I realise that). But it is what it is. 

All your work; whether it was open source or whether it was deep in the bowels or a proprietary company - they are all just going to go to models. As Ilya said, the models want to learn. They want to gorge on enormous amounts of data. The scaling laws have not plateaued out. Showing more and more novel data the models have never seen before still continue to make them smarter. So the data brokerage will continue. 

And I don’t know man… yes OpenAI and Anthropic will become trillion dollar companies and these researchers will get obscenely rich with their mansions at Twin Peak and Pacific Heights; but all this work is … in some way still going to improve humanity I guess. These AI tools are making all of humanity progress faster. New planets are getting discovered; mathematical algorithms are getting faster, new drugs are being discovered. 

Maybe this massive experiment of “pooling the world’s knowledge into one place to make an intelligence that no single brain could have ever been” is exactly what we need to go further from here. 

Don’t be grumpy about who is making money off what. If you are thinking “I could have done it too but I’m better than this”, then come on, go make the money if you want to; you cannot be jealous *and* also take the moral high ground.

So many takeaways, I have to share:

1. I'm not kidding when I say the "value per word" of this post is higher than every MBA program in America. 

(Another signal traditional education is cooked for 90%+ of jobs/industries.)

2. Great to see Silicon Valley finally taking notes from the ecom world. 

SV has historically been the best at creating products, and the worst at marketing. Ecom & affiliate marketers are the best marketers in the world, with info/agency marketers second. Meanwhile, most venture-backed founders don't even know how to run a simple retargeting ad or setup an automated email funnel.

3. WisperFlow hiring a 19 year old with a mid-IQ GPA to build this entire system is all the proof you need that the world has changed.

Nobody "owes" you a job. Either you build things that drive results or you pray for Universal Basic Income. Whether you think that's fair or not is irrelevant. That's the world we live in now. Get to work.

4. It continues to astound me how many creators don't have any idea how to measure the "value of their value."

When I see stuff like this, my first thought is always, "Why would creators accept such low payment terms?" And then I remember the vast majority of people have no clue how to make $1 online aside from social platforms paying them CPMs in exchange for attention. Marketers will arbitrage this all day long, because they understand LTV & biz models, whereas the average person only understands "I make content, get views."

candidates.text:
My hair has never looked or felt healthier since when I started blowdrying it which is insane because all my life I was told heat is the devil and it will destroy my hair!

Ofc heat damage is super real and you should ALWAYS use heat protectant and use your blow dryer on medium but what actually changed was understanding what happens to hair when it’s wet. 

Your hair is not just…hair you know? It’s porous, has a lot of internal structure and chemical bonds. When it’s wet, it absorbs water and swells and needs very gentle handling. Say you’re air drying your hair and it’s taking forever, and you run a brush through it, you ARE going to cause mechanical damage and breakage!

In a 2011 study done on hair samples, researchers washed and dried samples repeatedly and the air dried samples all took over 2 hours to dry and caused damage to the cell membrane complex (aka the glue that helps hold the hair’s cells together). 

Squeeze water out of your hair, put heat protectant, a bond repair if you’d like (I love k18), and dry on medium heat from about 10-15cm away. 

If air-drying works for you, carry on of course. But if you have thick hair that takes forever to dry like mine does, a gentle blow-dry is an option worth considering!

ChatGPT is creating new ad experiences and formats, which means there's no existing benchmark for how attribution compares to true incremental lift. That makes testing even more important, and we're excited to see the OpenAI team leaning into incrementality early.
